key_developments.event: Al-Aziz institutes formal teaching salaried by the Fatimid state.
Saladin suppresses Friday prayer at Al-Azhar — Ismaili dawa shuttered.
Baybars revives Al-Azhar as a Sunni teaching institution.
Mamluk endowments under al-Nasir Muhammad expand the four-school curriculum.

_quarry.description: Built between 970 and 972 by the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz as the congregational mosque of the new capital Cairo, Al-Azhar was developed under his successor al-Aziz into a centre for the propagation of Ismaili Shi'ism, becoming the doctrinal seat of the Fatimid da'wa. After Saladin's overthrow of the Fatimids in 1171, the institution was suppressed as a Shi'i centre but revived in 1266 under the Mamluk sultan Baybars as a Sunni school of Sunni jurisprudence and Qur'anic science. By the late Mamluk period it had become one of the principal centres of Sunni religious learning in the Islamic world.
